reason: The debris is hot, so cooling it seems a plausible first step toward forming the Moon.
expectation: The orbiting debris will lose heat and cool.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available partners instead, since the exact sequence is uncertain.

effect: Cooling was not the available first step; collisions spread the debris into a ring instead.
reaction: I was surprised the failed cooling attempt automatically advanced the debris.
reason: The ring must spread beyond the tidal disruption region for material to remain together and form the Moon.
expectation: Some ring material will move far enough out to begin gathering into the Moon.

effect: The ring produced growing moonlets beyond the disruptive tidal region; they can now gather into a larger body.
reaction: It is satisfying to see why distance from Earth matters for the clumps’ survival.
reason: Gravity within a dense swarm is a plausible way to gather the moonlets into a Moon.
expectation: The moonlets will merge into a larger Moon.

effect: The moonlets have gathered into a hot young Moon, which now needs to cool.
reaction: Seeing the moonlets become a substantial satellite is satisfying.
reason: Radiation can carry heat away from the young Moon and help its crust form.
expectation: The Moon will cool, allowing a crust to form.

effect: Cooling produced crystals in the lunar magma ocean, but the crust has not yet formed.
reaction: The distinction between sinking and floating minerals makes me curious how the crust gathers.
reason: Gravity should help separate minerals by density, allowing lighter crystals to contribute to a crust.

choice.combine: Crystals in the lunar magma ocean

expectation: The minerals will separate, with lighter crystals rising toward the lunar surface.

choice.inspect: Crystals in the lunar magma ocean

alternatives.reason: I could check their partners because the next step is not certain.

effect: The crystals combined with the young Moon to form a buoyant feldspar-rich layer; gravity was not the available partner.
reaction: The floating plagioclase makes the crust-forming process clearer.
reason: The layer is the clearest lead toward a lunar crust, but its next partner is uncertain.
expectation: The inspection should show how the layer can develop into a crust.

effect: The feldspar-rich layer cooled into an early lunar crust, completing the Moon goal; the remaining goal is to return debris to Earth.
reaction: The pale crust forming through further cooling is a satisfying conclusion to that sequence.
reason: The spreading ring contains debris that can fall inward, and the surviving Earth is the natural destination.
expectation: Inward-falling debris will return to Earth.

effect: Gravity turned the spreading ring into rock falling back toward Earth; it still needs to reach the planet.
reaction: The fallback path is clearer now, although my direct combination was premature.
reason: The surviving Earth is the destination of the falling rock.
expectation: The debris will return to Earth and complete the remaining goal.

effect: The falling debris reaccreted onto Earth, adding heat and reworking the planet, and completed the remaining goal.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the debris’s Earthward path resolved alongside the Moon’s formation.

mostWorthwhile.text: Forming the floating feldspar-rich layer was most worthwhile: it connected mineral buoyancy to the Moon’s early crust.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial cooling attempt was less worthwhile because collisions had to happen first, though the automatic feedback kept it moving.

surprise.text: I was surprised that a failed combination could automatically perform the sole available operation, first spreading the debris through collisions.

arbitrary.text: Combining the crystals with the hot young Moon rather than gravity was not obvious to me, although the resulting buoyant layer had a clear physical explanation.

continue.text: Yes. I would choose to continue to see how the remade Earth cools and develops, especially after learning that reaccretion adds heat.
